We just published the list of the 10 Worst Dow Stocks To Buy, and IBM (NYSE:IBM) ranks 9th on this list.

Yahoo Finance reported on November 5 that the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5% into correction territory. Chip stocks took the brunt of the damage, as the leading AI chipmaker fell 9% to pace Dow decliners and another chip designer plunged 17%, the outlet reported.

The slide erased the gains from a day earlier, when the Dow had jumped nearly 1,600 points after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Yahoo Finance wrote on November 4. Even so, the blue-chip index finished Thursday just 1.9% below its record closing high of 54,349 from early August, according to Yahoo Finance.

IBM (IBM): Software Is Speeding Up, Yet Analysts' Average Upside Is 5%
The Dow's Safe-Haven Run Cracks

For most of the week the Dow had looked like the sheltered corner of the market. Yahoo Finance reported on November 2 that the Dow edged up 0.4% while the Nasdaq dropped roughly 1% as investors rotated out of technology names and into consumer cyclical and financial services shares. One household consumer brand has divided opinion lately, and we covered why a well-known TV host is staying away from the sneaker maker after losing money on it.

On Thursday that cushion gave way, as the focus turned to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI buildout, and for the data centers driving it in particular, according to Yahoo Finance. Data center power and infrastructure stocks fell by double digits, and the Nasdaq 100 was recently more than 10% below its October closing high.

The reversal was fast. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at an equity research firm, pointed out that the VIX volatility index posted its biggest one-day jump in more than two years, Yahoo Finance reported on November 5. It took the Nasdaq just six minutes to erase its entire post-election rally.

A Jobs Report Steadies the Tape

Friday brought a partial rebound. Yahoo Finance reported on November 6 that the U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, and the Nasdaq gained 1.9% while the S&P 500 rose 1% and the Dow added 0.1%. You might also be interested in reading our piece on why a billionaire money manager and a TV host both still like the iPhone maker.

The stronger jobs data lifted Treasury yields and kept Federal Reserve policy at the center of market attention, Reuters reported on November 6, as the price-weighted index of 30 major U.S. companies held roughly flat.

IBM's average upside potential, based on analysts' average price target, is 5%. It has a short interest of 2.11% and had 74 hedge fund holders as of Q2 2026.

title: He Inherited 8,000 IBM Shares Worth Nearly $2 Million at 52. The Often Overlooked IRS Rule That Decides Whether Most of It Is Taxed as Income or a Capital Gain

He Inherited 8,000 IBM Shares Worth Nearly $2 Million at 52. The Often Overlooked IRS Rule That Decides Whether Most of It Is Taxed as Income or a Capital Gain
AJ Tiarsmith

IBM
Trade IBM on Coinbase

Quick Read

An heir who takes IBM shares in kind from a 401(k) pays ordinary income tax only on the $231,000 basis, leaving $1.7 million of growth untaxed until sale.

Rolling the 401(k) into an inherited IRA closes the NUA window for good, and every dollar withdrawn within 10 years is taxed as ordinary income.

NUA gets missed because heirs consolidate into an IRA, and the CPA Journal says "once the qualified plan is moved to an IRA, the opportunity for NUA is lost."

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

If your parent left you a 401(k) full of company stock, the default paperwork could cost you a fortune. A little-known IRS rule called net unrealized appreciation (NUA) lets an heir take employer stock out of an inherited 401(k) and pay capital gains tax on most of it instead of ordinary income tax. Most heirs never hear about it until the money has already moved.

PeopleImages / Shutterstock.com
A Hypothetical $2 Million Inheritance Inside a 401(k)

This example is hypothetical. It exists to show how the rule works. A son, 52, is the named beneficiary of his late father's 401(k). The father spent 33 years as a systems engineer at IBM (NYSE:IBM) and bought IBM stock inside the plan throughout his career. Those purchases, plus IBM's two-for-one stock splits declared in January 1997 and January 1999 (per IBM's filings), left the plan holding 8,000 shares with a cost basis of $231,000.

At IBM's price of $244.89 as of 2:37 PM ET on Nov. 6, 2026, the shares are worth $1,959,120. That leaves $1,728,120 of net unrealized appreciation, or 88.2% of the position. The value moves with IBM's stock price.

------

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›

------

Two Paths, Two Very Different Tax Bills

The default: an inherited IRA. Most heirs roll the balance into an inherited IRA. The son is more than 10 years younger than his father, so he falls outside the eligible designated beneficiary category for someone "not more than 10 years younger" than the owner. That means he must empty the account by the end of the tenth year after the year his father died, per the IRS. Every dollar he withdraws, growth included, counts as ordinary income.

title: Better Dividend Stock: Cisco vs. IBM

Better Dividend Stock: Cisco vs. IBM

CSCO
IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Better Dividend Stock: Cisco vs. IBM ©@dotshock via Canva
Key Takeaways

IBM yields 2.7%, against 1.7% for Cisco Systems.

IBM's dividend took 43% of its trailing-12-month free cash flow, against 51% at Cisco.

Cisco's revenue grew 12% in fiscal 2026 and its dividend has risen for 15 straight years, while IBM's dividend has grown just 0.6% a year since fiscal 2020.

IBM carries net debt of 3.1x EBITDA, against 0.8x at Cisco.

International Business Machines (IBM:NYSE) raised its free cash flow outlook on Oct. 21. It now expects more than $1 billion of growth this year. The stock still fell 5% after hours, as investors questioned whether its software rebound would last.

Cisco Systems (CSCO:NASDAQ) has the reverse worry. Its revenue grew 12% in fiscal 2026, and on Nov. 5 Morgan Stanley downgraded it to Equal-Weight from Overweight, citing its valuation and AI-related pressure on gross margin.

For anyone buying for income, the question is which of these dividends is the better one to own.

Source: TIKR, Nov. 5, 2026; records from each company's own release or call.

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

Cisco has the growth

Cisco's revenue grew 12% to $63.3 billion in fiscal 2026, the year ended July 25. It guides for $72.2 billion to $73.4 billion in fiscal 2027. It took $9.3 billion of AI infrastructure orders from hyperscalers over fiscal 2026. As CEO Chuck Robbins put it on the fourth-quarter call, "We believe the accelerating adoption of agentic AI is fueling a networking super cycle."

That business has funded 15 straight years of raises. Cisco's dividend is well covered, taking 51% of free cash flow over the trailing-12 months to July 25, 2026. Dividends paid rose every year for a decade, while free cash flow swung between $10.2 billion and $19.0 billion:

Cisco Systems (CSCO): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2017–2026 (years to July) (TIKR)

Even in fiscal 2024, its tightest year, the dividend took a manageable 62.5%.

The raises are modest, though: 2.6% a year from fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2026, from $1.46 to $1.66 a share. And Cisco's product gross margin fell 270 basis points in the fourth quarter because of a heavier hardware mix and memory costs. That's the same pressure Morgan Stanley cited.

IBM has the bigger check

IBM is the mirror image, with slower sales growth and a bigger payout. Third-quarter revenue rose 5% to $17.1 billion. Software was up 8% and Red Hat up 11%, while IBM Z revenue fell 20% against a strong launch period a year earlier. Doubts about that growth are why the stock fell on Oct. 21.

title: What Just Happened To Accenture Stock?
detail:
What Just Happened To Accenture Stock?
Trefis Team
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 5:41 PM CST 3 min read
ACN
^GSPC
IBM
CTSH
BAH

Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Accenture (ACN) stock gained 49.9% from May 9 to November 5, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.08% over the same period. The shares logged their biggest one-day gain of the past year on October 1, climbing 15.8% when Accenture reported its fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 results and gave its outlook for fiscal 2027. What did that report show about the business?

From June's Low To October's Forecast-Beating Report

Accenture posted fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $18.7 billion, up 7% in local currency. Management said this result topped the high end of its guided range. Clients signed $22.2 billion of new bookings during the quarter. Managed services generated $9.4 billion of the quarter's revenue and booked a record $12.8 billion of new work.

The six-month gain also includes a steep drop. Shares fell 18.0% on June 18, the day of Accenture's fiscal third-quarter earnings call, and closed at their lowest level of the past year on June 30. On that call, management lowered its full-year revenue growth outlook to 3% to 4% in local currency.

Most of the six-month gain came after the October report. From October 7 to November 5, the shares returned 35.9%, while the S&P 500 lost 5.7%. Counting the report day itself, the share price is up 45.8% since the September 30 close. Accenture's peers also rose, though less: Cognizant gained 30% from May 9 to November 5.

The S&P 500's 5.7% slide included a 4.4% drop on November 5. Here's how the market did after 21 days like it.

Accenture Now Trades At Nearly Double June's P/E

At the end of June, Accenture stock traded at 9.8 times its twelve-month earnings, its lowest quarterly reading since fiscal 2017. At the November 5 close, it traded at 19.1 times, still below the S&P 500's 22.9 times.

Accenture's profit grew far less than its share price. Net income for fiscal 2026 was $8.37 billion, against $7.68 billion in fiscal 2025. The share price rise since June therefore comes mostly from a higher price on Accenture's profit, and only a little from a larger profit.

Management Still Expects Growth Near Last Year's Pace

Management expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 3% to 6% in local currency, a range centered just below the 5% local-currency growth Accenture posted in fiscal 2026. Reported growth had already eased, with fiscal 2026 revenue rising 6.5% against 7.4% in fiscal 2025. In other words, Accenture's growth is about where it was before its shares rose, or a little slower. At its October 14 Investor Day, though, Accenture outlined a multiyear strategy aimed at faster growth, and some analysts raised their price targets afterward.
